Incidents

1945 plane crash

Main article: B-25 Empire State Building crash

At 9:40 am on July 28, 1945, a North American B-25 Mitchell bomber, piloted in thick fog by Lieutenant Colonel William Franklin Smith Jr.,[390] crashed into the north side of the Empire State Building between the 79th and 80th floors (then the offices of the National Catholic Welfare Council).[35][56] One engine completely penetrated the building, landing on the roof of a nearby building where it started a fire that destroyed a penthouse.[385][391][392] The other engine and part of the landing gear plummeted down an elevator shaft, causing a fire that was extinguished in 40 minutes. Fourteen people were killed in the incident.[285][198][392] Elevator operator Betty Lou Oliver fell 75 stories and survived, which still holds the Guinness World Record for the longest survived elevator fall recorded.[393]

Despite the damage and loss of life, many floors were open two days later.[285][286] The crash helped spur the passage of the long-pending Federal Tort Claims Act of 1946, as well as the insertion of retroactive provisions into the law, allowing people to sue the government for the incident.[394] Also as a result of the crash, the Civil Aeronautics Administration enacted strict regulations regarding flying over New York City, setting a minimum flying altitude of 2,500 feet (760 m) above sea level regardless of the weather conditions.[395][285]

A year later, on July 24, 1946, another airplane narrowly missed striking the building. The unidentified twin-engine plane scraped past the observation deck, frightening the tourists there.[396]

2000 elevator plunge

On January 24, 2000, an elevator in the building suddenly descended 40 stories after a cable that controlled the cabin's maximum speed was severed.[397] The elevator fell from the 44th floor to the fourth floor, where a narrowed elevator shaft provided a second safety system. Despite the 40-floor fall, both of the passengers in the cabin at the time were only slightly injured. After the fall, building inspectors reviewed all of the building's elevators.[398]

Suicide attempts

Because of the building's iconic status, it and other Midtown landmarks are common locations for suicide attempts.[399] More than 30 people have attempted suicide over the years by jumping from the upper parts of the building, with most attempts being successful.[400][401]

The first suicide from the building occurred on April 7, 1931, before it was even completed, when a carpenter who had been laid off went to the 58th floor and jumped.[402] The first suicide after the building's opening occurred from the 86th floor observatory in February 1935, when Irma P. Eberhardt fell 1,029 feet (314 m) onto a marquee sign.[403] On December 16, 1943, William Lloyd Rambo jumped to his death from the 86th floor, landing amidst Christmas shoppers on the street below.[404] In the early morning of September 27, 1946, shell-shocked Marine Douglas W. Brashear Jr. jumped from the 76th-floor window of the Grant Advertising Agency; police found his shoes 50 feet (15 m) from his body.[405]

On May 1, 1947, Evelyn McHale leaped to her death from the 86th-floor observation deck and landed on a limousine parked at the curb. Photography student Robert Wiles took a photo of McHale's oddly intact corpse a few minutes after her death. The police found a suicide note among possessions that she left on the observation deck: "He is much better off without me.... I wouldn't make a good wife for anybody". The photo ran in the May 12, 1947, edition of Life magazine[406] and is often referred to as "The Most Beautiful Suicide". It was later used by visual artist Andy Warhol in one of his prints entitled Suicide (Fallen Body).[407] A 7-foot (2.1 m) mesh fence was put up around the 86th floor terrace in December 1947 after five people tried to jump during three weeks in October and November of that year.[408][409] By then, sixteen people had died from suicide jumps.[408]

Only one person has jumped from the upper observatory: Frederick Eckert of Astoria, Queens, who ran past a guard in the enclosed 102nd-floor gallery on November 3, 1932. He jumped a gate leading to an outdoor catwalk intended for dirigible passengers, dying when he landed on the 86th-floor deck.[410]

Two people have survived falls by not falling more than a floor. On December 2, 1979, Elvita Adams jumped from the 86th floor, only to be blown back onto a ledge on the 85th floor by a gust of wind and left with a broken hip.[411][412][413] On April 25, 2013, a man fell from the 86th floor observation deck, but he landed alive with minor injuries on an 85th-floor ledge where security guards brought him inside and paramedics transferred him to a hospital for a psychiatric evaluation.[414]

Shootings

Two fatal shootings have occurred in the direct vicinity of the Empire State Building. Abu Kamal, a 69-year-old Palestinian teacher, shot seven people on the 86th floor observation deck during the afternoon of February 23, 1997. He killed one person and wounded six others before committing suicide.[415] Kamal reportedly committed the shooting in response to events happening in Palestine and Israel.[416]

On the morning of August 24, 2012, 58-year-old Jeffrey T. Johnson shot and killed a former co-worker on the building's Fifth Avenue sidewalk. He had been laid off from his job in 2011. Two police officers confronted the gunman, and he aimed his firearm at them. They responded by firing 16 shots, killing him but also wounding nine bystanders. Most of the injured were hit by bullet fragments, although three took direct hits from bullets.[15][417]

Impact

As the tallest building in the world and the first one to exceed 100 floors, the Empire State Building immediately became an icon of the city and of the nation.[250][32][315] In 2013, Time magazine noted that the Empire State Building "seems to completely embody the city it has become synonymous with".[418] The historian John Tauranac called it "'the' twentieth-century New York building", despite the existence of taller and more modernist buildings.[419]

The New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission voted to designate the building and its lobby as city landmarks on May 19, 1981,[318][319] citing the historic nature of the first and second floors, as well as "the fixtures and interior components" of the upper floors.[420] The New York City Planning Commission endorsed the landmark status.[421] The building became a National Historic Landmark in 1986[10][422][423] in close alignment with the New York City Landmarks report.[422] The Empire State Building was added to the National Register of Historic Places the following year due to its architectural significance.[424]

Contemporary reception

Early architectural critics also focused on the Empire State Building's exterior ornamentation.[36] Architectural critic Talbot Hamlin wrote in 1931, "That it is the world's tallest building is purely incidental."[425] George Shepard Chappell, writing in The New Yorker under the pseudonym "T-Square", wrote the same year that the Empire State Building had a "palpably enormous" appeal to the general public, and that "its difference and distinction [lay] in the extreme sensitiveness of its entire design".[36][426] Edmund Wilson of The New Republic wrote that the building's neutral color palette made it "New York's handsomest skyscraper".[321]

Architectural critics also wrote negatively of the mast, especially in light of its failure to become a real air terminal. Chappell called the mast "a silly gesture", and Lewis Mumford called it "a public comfort station for migratory birds".[36] Nevertheless, architecture critic Douglas Haskell said the Empire State Building's appeal came from the fact that it was "caught at the exact moment of transition—caught between metal and stone, between the idea of 'monumental mass' and that of airy volume, between handicraft and machine design, and in the swing from what was essentially handicraft to what will be essentially industrial methods of fabrication."[427]

As icon

Early in the building's history, travel companies such as Short Line Motor Coach Service and New York Central Railroad used the building as an icon to symbolize the city.[428] In a 1932 survey of 50 American architects, fourteen ranked the Empire State Building as the United States' best building; the Empire State Building received more votes than any building except the Lincoln Memorial.[429][430] After the construction of the first World Trade Center, architect Paul Goldberger noted that the Empire State Building "is famous for being tall, but it is good enough to be famous for being good."[114]

As an icon of the United States, it is also very popular among Americans. In a 2007 survey, the American Institute of Architects found that the Empire State Building was "America's favorite building".[431] The building was originally a symbol of hope in a country devastated by the Depression, as well as a work of accomplishment by newer immigrants.[250] The writer Benjamin Flowers states that the Empire State was "a building intended to celebrate a new America, built by men (both clients and construction workers) who were themselves new Americans."[245] The architectural critic Jonathan Glancey refers to the building as an "icon of American design".[363] Additionally, in 2007, the Empire State Building was first on the AIA's List of America's Favorite Architecture.[432]

The Empire State Building has been hailed as an example of a "wonder of the world" due to the massive effort expended during construction.[419] The Washington Star listed it as part of one of the "seven wonders of the modern world" in 1931, while Holiday magazine wrote in 1958 that the Empire State's height would be taller than the combined heights of the Eiffel Tower and the Great Pyramid of Giza.[419] The American Society of Civil Engineers also declared the building "A Modern Civil Engineering Wonder of the United States" in 1958[297] and one of the Seven Wonders of the Modern World in 1994.[433] Ron Miller, in a 2010 book, also described the Empire State Building as one of the "seven wonders of engineering".[434] It has often been called the Eighth Wonder of the World as well, an appellation that it has held since shortly after opening.[197][283][435] The panels installed in the lobby in 1963 reflected this, showing the seven original wonders alongside the Empire State Building.[97] The Empire State Building also became the standard of reference to describe the height and length of other structures globally, both natural and human-made.[436]

The building has also inspired replicas. The New York-New York Hotel and Casino in Paradise, Nevada, contains the "Empire Tower",[437] a 47-story replica of the Empire State Building.[438][439] A portion of the hotel's interior was also designed to resemble the Empire State Building's interior.[438]

In media

Main article: Empire State Building in popular culture

As an icon of New York City, the Empire State Building has been featured in various films, books, TV shows, and video games. According to the building's official website, more than 250 movies contain depictions of the Empire State Building.[440] In his book about the building, John Tauranac writes that its first documented appearance in popular culture was Swiss Family Manhattan, a 1932 children's story by Christopher Morley.[441] A year later, the film King Kong depicted Kong, a giant stop motion ape that climbs the Empire State Building during the film's climax,[259][260][442] bringing the building into the popular imagination.[56][442] Later movies such as An Affair to Remember (1957), Sleepless in Seattle (1993), and Independence Day (1996) also prominently featured the building.[443][440] The building has also been featured in other works, such as "Daleks in Manhattan", a 2007 episode of the TV series Doctor Who;[443] and Empire, an eight-hour black-and-white silent film by Andy Warhol,[443] which was later added to the Library of Congress's National Film Registry.[444]

Throughout its history, the Empire State Building has welcomed celebrities, royalty, and dignitaries to visit the observation deck. From celebrities like Taylor Swift and Zendaya to royalty such as Prince William, the Empire State Building hosts notable figures every year.[445]

Empire State Building Run-Up

The Empire State Building Run-Up, a foot race from ground level to the 86th-floor observation deck, has been held annually since 1978.[446] It is organized by NYCRUNS.[447] Its participants are referred to both as runners and as climbers, and are often tower running enthusiasts. The race covers a vertical distance of 1,050 ft (320 m) and takes in 1,576 steps. The record time is 9 minutes and 33 seconds, achieved by Australian professional cyclist Paul Crake in 2003, at a climbing rate of 6,593 ft (2,010 m) per hour.[448][449]

This system of setbacks would continue until the tower reaches a floor level in which that level's floor area was 25% that of the ground level's area. After that 25% threshold was reached, the building could rise without restriction.[42][43][44] The 1916 Zoning Act was amended in 1961 so that buildings erected thereafter could not exceed a floor area ratio that was calculated for each zoning district.[45] The maximum ratio for the Empire State Building's district is 15, unless it includes a public plaza.[46] A grandfather clause permits preexisting structures to continue under the old rule. Therefore, the Empire State Building's floor area ratio of 25 cannot be duplicated, or even approached, by a new building in that district.[47]
